summary: Defines a way for LDP routers to advertise optional enhancements when a session starts. As new features are proposed, this lets peers learn what the other supports.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives LDP speakers a common way to announce optional features. They can report capabilities when a session starts and, when supported by the peer, update that list later.

questions: how do ldp peers negotiate enhancements
what is the ldp capability message
how do ldp peers negotiate features
what is dynamic capability announcement in ldp
subtitle: LDP peers can advertise supported enhancements at setup and announce changes while a session is active.

tldr.problem: LDP enhancements need a consistent way for peers to learn which features the other speaker can process.
tldr.mechanism: Initialization messages can carry Capability Parameters, and a Capability message can advertise or withdraw them after setup when the peer supports dynamic announcements.
tldr.outcome: Enhancement specifications can define their own capability data and code points, while older peers retain base LDP behavior. RFC 5561 updates RFC 5036.

today: RFC 5561 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2009. It updates RFC 5036, the LDP Specification.

sections.title: Why LDP Needs Capabilities
sections.content:
Several enhancements to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) had been proposed, including graceful restart, fault tolerance, multicast extensions, and Layer 2 circuit signaling. RFC 5561 defines a shared mechanism to advertise enhancements at session setup and to enable or disable them after setup.

An advertisement tells a peer that the speaker can receive and process the associated enhancement. Not every LDP enhancement needs capability advertisement; the enhancement's specification determines whether it is required.
sections.plainLanguage: LDP has optional enhancements, and peers need a consistent way to state which ones they support. This RFC defines that announcement mechanism.

sections.title: Advertising and Withdrawing Features
sections.content:
At session setup, a speaker MAY include a Capability Parameter in its Initialization message. Advertising a capability means the speaker will perform the protocol actions required by that enhancement.

The Dynamic Capability Announcement capability tells a peer that the speaker can process later changes. If the peer advertised it during initialization, a speaker MAY send a Capability message to advertise or withdraw capabilities while the session remains active.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers can list supported capabilities when they connect. Later changes are sent only when the other peer said it can process capability updates.

sections.title: Capability Parameter Fields
sections.content:
A Capability Parameter is an optional TLV in an Initialization or Capability message. It includes the unknown-TLV bit (U), a forward-unknown bit (F), a TLV code point, a length, a state bit (S), reserved bits, and optional capability data. The F bit MUST be zero because these messages are not forwarded.

The S bit is 1 when the sender advertises a capability and 0 when it withdraws one. Each capability's specification defines its U-bit behavior and how to interpret any capability data. A speaker MUST NOT include the same capability twice in one message.
sections.plainLanguage: Each capability TLV identifies a feature and says whether it is active or withdrawn. Its own specification explains how peers should handle unknown features and extra data.

sections.title: The Capability Message
sections.content:
The Capability message has code point 0x0202. It carries a message ID and one or more Capability Parameter TLVs; each TLV's S bit gives the new state for that capability.

Backward Compatibility TLVs may still appear in Initialization messages, where their presence has the same meaning as an advertised capability. They MUST NOT appear in a Capability message. A receiver SHOULD ignore them if they are included there and continue processing the other parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: A Capability message reports changes after a session begins. Older initialization parameters remain supported for compatibility, but they are not used in these update messages.

sections.title: Peer Behavior and Unknown Capabilities
sections.content:
The S bit in a Capability Parameter in an Initialization message MUST be 1 and SHOULD be ignored when received. A speaker learns the peer's capabilities from its Initialization message and MAY use an enhancement after confirming the peer enabled it.

A speaker MUST NOT send a Capability message unless its peer advertised Dynamic Capability Announcement during initialization. If a receiver does not understand a capability, U=1 means it MUST silently ignore the parameter; U=0 means it SHOULD send an Unsupported Capability notification and terminate the session.
sections.plainLanguage: A speaker can use an enhancement after it learns that the peer enabled it. For unknown capabilities, the U bit determines whether the peer ignores the item or ends the session.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
For backward compatibility, an RFC 5036-compliant peer is treated as having IPv4 label distribution enabled unless it is explicitly disabled. Existing extensions may continue using their older initialization TLVs.

The security framework and considerations for base LDP and MPLS apply to this mechanism. RFC 5561 says it adds no separate security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Older LDP peers keep the base IPv4 label-distribution behavior. The RFC relies on the security guidance already defined for LDP and MPLS.
